arXiv:2511.07112v1 [cs.CL] 10 Nov 2025

More Agents Helps but Adversarial Robustness Gap Persists

*Equal contribution
Abstract

When LLM agents work together, they seem to be more powerful than a single LLM in mathematical question answering. However, are they also more robust to adversarial inputs? We investigate this question using adversarially perturbed math questions. These perturbations include punctuation noise with three intensities (10%10\%, 30%30\%, 50%50\%), plus real-world and human-like typos (WikiTypo, R2ATA). Using a unified sampling-and-voting framework (Agent Forest), we evaluate six open-source models (Qwen3-4B/14B, Llama3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma3-4B/12B) across four benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, MMLU–Math, MultiArith), with various numbers of agents n∈{1,2,5,10,15,20,25}n\in\{1,2,5,10,15,20,25\}. Our findings show that (1) Noise type matters: punctuation noise harm scales with its severity, and the human typos remain the dominant bottleneck, yielding the largest gaps to Clean accuracy and the highest ASR even with a large number of agents. And (2) Collaboration reliably improves accuracy as the number of agents, nn, increases, with the largest gains from n=1n{=}1 to n=5n{=}5 and diminishing returns beyond n≈10n{\approx}10. However, the adversarial robustness gap persists regardless of the agent count.

Keywords: LLM agents, adversarial robustness, math question answering

Abstract content

1.  Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress in solving a variety of reasoning-intensive tasks Zhao et al. (2025), including mathematical problem solving. Beyond simply scaling model size, recent work shows that treating multiple LLM instances as agents and combining their outputs through debate, voting, or self-consistency can substantially boost performance. Li et al. (2024) demonstrate that even a simple sampling-and-voting strategy, essentially allowing multiple agents to propose answers and then aggregating them, can rival more sophisticated collaborative frameworks. These findings suggest that collaboration between agents is a powerful and relatively simple way to enhance reasoning accuracy. At the same time, another body of research highlights a major weakness of LLMs: their fragility when inputs are perturbed. While the semantic meaning of a math problem may remain unchanged, minor surface-level changes, such as synonym replacements Shi et al. (2023b), typos Gemma Team et al. (2024), or even random punctuation insertions, can significantly reduce model accuracy. For instance, Abedin et al. (2025) show that inserting punctuation noise, despite leaving the problem content intact, can cause accuracy drops on well-established benchmarks like GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021) and MultiArith Roy and Roth (2016). These two perspectives converge on an important open question: If multiple agents can enhance reasoning performance on Clean inputs, can they also improve robustness under noisy conditions? Understanding whether ensemble-based multi-agent setups show resilience to noise would provide valuable insights for designing more reliable and trustworthy LLM systems.

To address this gap, we investigate the robustness of Agent Forest (a multi-LLM-agent setup) to adversarially perturbed math questions. We develop a taxonomy of noise types for adversarial modification and systematically introduce them across multiple reasoning datasets for mathematical question answering, enabling a controlled evaluation of their impact. We use ArithmAttack Abedin et al. (2025) to generate synthetic noise, while for real-world noise we rely on natural typos from Wikipedia Aliakbarzadeh et al. (2025) and adversarial perturbations introduced by the Adversarial Typo Attack Gan et al. (2024). We assess the impact of input noise perturbations on open-source LLMs, specifically Qwen Yang et al. (2025), Llama Dubey et al. (2024), Mistral Jiang et al. (2023), and Gemma Gemma Team et al. (2025), across multiple parameter scales. By doing so, we evaluate not only how noise affects individual models but also whether multi-agent collaboration enhances resilience and preserves reasoning accuracy in the presence of such perturbations.

Figure 1 gives an overview of the results of our investigation. Across all experiments, we observe a consistent, monotonic gain from increasing the number of collaborating agents. Averaged over datasets and models, accuracy rises from 0.65790.6579 with a single agent to 0.77400.7740 with 2525 agents, with the largest jump occurring between o​n​eone and f​i​v​efive agents and clear diminishing returns beyond 1010. The relative ordering of noise conditions is stable: With the Clean performance at the top, Punct-1010 (i.e., inserting punctuation noise in as many spaces as 1010 percent of the question length) causes a consistent accuracy drop, then even larger drops are caused by Punct-3030 and Punct-5050, while WikiTypo is consistently the most challenging, causing a drop of 8%8\% across all the settings with different numbers of agents. R2ATA causes a slightly larger drop than Punct-1010 in our aggregate.

2.  Related Work

Recent work has shown that current open-source large language models (LLMs) exhibit limited resilience to naturally occurring input noise, such as spelling mistakes, typographical errors, and minor punctuation artifacts, raising serious concerns about their reliability in real-world deployments Dong et al. (2023); Abedin et al. (2025). A substantial body of research has analyzed the impact of input perturbations across multiple granularities. At the character level, studies examine misspellings and typos Gao et al. (2018); Li et al. (2018); at the word level, attacks involve synonym substitution or word shuffling Garg and Ramakrishnan (2020); Moradi and Samwald (2021); and at the sentence level, robustness is tested via paraphrasing or insertion of irrelevant context Shi et al. (2023a); Lanham et al. (2023). Even seemingly innocuous changes, such as random punctuation insertion, have been shown to significantly degrade performance Abedin et al. (2025). These perturbations have been evaluated across a range of tasks and settings. Prior analyses of LLMs under noisy inputs include text classification Eger and Benz (2020), natural language inference Formento et al. (2021); Formento et al. (2023), and multilingual scenarios Aliakbarzadeh et al. (2025), offering valuable insights into task-specific vulnerabilities.

In parallel, a growing line of work Talebirad and Nadiri (2023); Seo et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025) demonstrates that multi-agent or ensemble approaches, where multiple LLM instances generate and aggregate responses, can substantially boost reasoning performance on Clean inputs. Lu et al. (2024) show that simple strategies like self-consistency or majority voting often rival more complex debate frameworks, and ensembles of smaller models match or exceed the performance of much larger single models.

Helmi (2025b) provide preliminary evidence that multi-agent reasoning can degrade under high noise levels, highlighting a potential vulnerability. Nevertheless, a systematic evaluation across diverse noise types, reasoning tasks, and agent scales has not yet been conducted. Together, these observations reveal a critical gap: while both noise robustness and multi-agent collaboration are active research areas, their intersection, how ensemble-based reasoning fares under diverse, realistic input corruptions, has not been systematically explored.

3.  Methodology

Figure 2 depicts our pipeline for evaluating the adversarial robustness of LLMs from noisy dataset generation to answer extraction.

3.1.  Noisy Dataset Creation

To systematically analyze the influence of noise on multi-agent LLMs, we introduce a taxonomy that distinguishes between synthetic noise and human-like noise. This taxonomy enables a structured evaluation of model performance under both artificially generated perturbations and noise patterns that more closely resemble human input.

Synthetic noise.

Following ArithmAttack Abedin et al. (2025), we implement synthetic noise with punctuation insertion, where symbols from the set {".", ",", "!", "?", ";", ":"} are randomly added to sentences. To study the effect of perturbation strength, each noise type is applied at three intensity levels (10%10\%, 30%30\%, and 50%50\%), allowing a controlled analysis of model performance under progressively noisier conditions.

Human-like noise.

To mimic realistic human errors, we consider two complementary approaches. The first is the Adversarial Typo Attack (ATA) Gan et al. (2024), which evaluates the robustness of LLMs to typographical errors by iteratively introducing common character-level mistakes typically caused by keyboard usage. These include letter duplication, character substitution, deletion, or insertion, and removal of spaces, all targeted toward words that are important for the query, with the goal of degrading model performance. For this, we rely on the R2ATA benchmark, which applies ATA to GSM8K, BBH, and MMLU tasks. The second approach leverages naturally occurring spelling mistakes extracted from Wikipedia edit histories Aliakbarzadeh et al. (2025). Specifically, we use the WikiTypo dictionary, which provides a collection of real-world human spelling errors, to replace words in the datasets with authentic typo variants.

3.2.  Agent Forest

We evaluate multi-agent performance using Agent Forest Li et al. (2024), which consists of two phases: sampling and voting. For each question xx from a dataset, we query the same base model ℳ\mathcal{M} multiple times with independent random seeds and fixed decoding settings. Each call acts as one agent and produces one candidate solution sis_{i}. After NN calls we obtain the set of candidates S={s1,…,sN}S=\{s_{1},\dots,s_{N}\}.

Answer extraction and normalization.

For arithmetic datasets, we extract the final numeric answer from each sis_{i} using simple patterns that look for common markers such as Answer or \boxed{}. We then extract the value by removing formatting artifacts, converting textual numbers to numerals, and standardizing whitespace. This yields a canonical answer canon⁡(si)\mathrm{canon}(s_{i}) for each sample.

Aggregation by voting.

To specify the final answer, we aggregate candidates by majority vote over canonical answers.

Protocol and replication.

For every model and dataset, we generate exactly 2525 independent single-agent outputs per question with fixed decoding parameters. To study different agent counts n∈{1,2,5,10,15,20,25}n\in\{1,2,5,10,15,20,25\}, we partition the 2525 samples into ⌊25/n⌋\lfloor 25/n\rfloor disjoint groups of size nn in their generation order. Each group forms one independent nn agent ensemble whose vote yields one prediction for that question. Thus we obtain 2525 independent predictions for n=1n=1, 1212 for n=2n=2, 55 for n=5n=5, and 22 for n=10n=10. For n=15n=15, n=20n=20, and n=25n=25, only one ensemble is available, so we use the first nn outputs. At the dataset level, we compute accuracy for each independent group and report the mean and the standard deviation across groups when multiple groups exist. No fine-tuning or task-specific supervision is used, and decoding settings are identical for Clean and noisy inputs so that any change in accuracy is attributable to aggregation by Agent Forest.

3.3.  Evaluation Metrics

We report accuracy and Attack Success Rate (ASR). Let 𝒟={(xi,yi)}i=1m\mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m} be a data set with gold answers yiy_{i}. Let fnf_{n} denote the nn agent ensemble predictor that maps an input xx to a single answer by Agent Forest voting as defined in Section 3.2. The metric is:

Accuracy.

Clean accuracy for nn agents:

Acc(n)=1m∑i=1m[fn(xi)=yi].\mathrm{Acc}(n)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\,f_{n}(x_{i})=y_{i}\,\right].

Attack Success Rate (ASR).

ASR measures the fraction of originally correct predictions that are flipped to incorrect after applying the noise. Formally,

ASR⁡(n)=∑i=1m[fn(A(xi))≠yi]∑i=1m[fn(xi)=yi].\mathrm{ASR}(n)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\,f_{n}(A(x_{i}))\neq y_{i}\,\right]}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\,f_{n}(x_{i})=y_{i}\,\right]}.

ASR is thus defined on the subset of items that the model with nn agents solves correctly in the Clean setting and takes values in [0,1][0,1]. A lower value indicates better robustness.

Reporting.

As described in Section 3.2, for each model and dataset, we generate 2525 independent single-agent outputs per question and form disjoint groups to realize different agent counts n∈{1,2,5,10,15,20,25}n\in\{1,2,5,10,15,20,25\}. For n∈{1,2,5,10}n\in\{1,2,5,10\} this yields multiple independent groups; we compute Acc\mathrm{Acc} and ASR\mathrm{ASR} for each group and report the mean and the standard deviation across groups. For n∈{15,20,25}n\in\{15,20,25\} only one group is available; we report the single value.

4.  Experiments

All experiments were executed on HPC GPU Cluster 8 x NVIDIA GA100 [A100] GPUs with 80GB, running under CUDA 12.2. We used Python 3.10 with the PyTorch 2.2 and HuggingFace Transformers Wolf et al. (2020) libraries. For efficient inference, we employed vLLM Kwon et al. (2023), which allows fast batched decoding for large-scale evaluation.

4.1.  Datasets

Evaluation of mathematical reasoning capabilities is conducted across four established benchmarks: GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021), MATH Hendrycks et al. (2021b), the mathematics subset of MMLU Hendrycks et al. (2021a), and MultiArith Roy and Roth (2016). This selection provides a comprehensive assessment spanning difficulty levels from basic arithmetic to advanced competition problems while incorporating both open-ended and multiple-choice formats.

GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021) contains 8.5K linguistically diverse grade school math word problems, with evaluation performed on the standard 1.3K test questions requiring multi-step arithmetic reasoning. Its broad adoption as a mathematical problem-solving benchmark offers a standard reference point for studying reasoning robustness under input noise.

The MATH dataset Hendrycks et al. (2021b) consists of 12.5K challenging mathematics competition problems covering advanced topics, including algebra, geometry, and number theory. These problems require symbolic manipulation and multi-step derivations, enabling assessment of how adversarial noise affects complex problem-solving capabilities compared to elementary-level reasoning.

Evaluation using MMLU Hendrycks et al. (2021a) focuses specifically on the mathematics subsets, which provide multiple-choice questions testing factual recall and mathematical reasoning. This format complements the open-ended generation tasks from other datasets.

MultiArith Roy and Roth (2016) consists of 600 arithmetic word problems requiring multi-step operations, with evaluation on the standard 180-question test set. This dataset serves as a lightweight benchmark for studying noise effects on simple yet compositional reasoning tasks.

4.2.  Models

To evaluate a diverse range of capabilities while maintaining computational efficiency, a selection of modern open-weight language models of varying parameter sizes was chosen for evaluation to analyze the impact of model scale. The models comprise Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Qwen3-14B-Instruct Yang et al. (2025), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct Dubey et al. (2024), Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 Jiang et al. (2023), along with Gemma3-4B-IT and Gemma3-12B-IT Gemma Team et al. (2025). These models will be subsequently referred to as Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-14B, Llama3.1, Mistral-7B, Gemma3-4B, and Gemma3-12B, respectively.

5.  Results

The overall trends, regarding the impact of each adversarial perturbation method, show themselves when we average the results over datasets and models. This can be seen in Figure 1, depicting that all the methods cause a consistent robustness gap, with WikiTypo having the largest one. In the following, we report the results and the trends across the adversarial models, datasets, and adversarial noise, respectively.

5.1.  Models

Figure 3 (also Table 1 in detail) presents the impact of input perturbations across models and agent counts. Increasing the number of agents reliably improves performance under all noise types. The largest improvements occur between n=1n{=}1 and n=5n{=}5, with diminishing returns beyond n≥10n{\geq}10. At the same time, ASR decreases as the agent count grows (Figure 4), indicating that majority voting not only boosts overall accuracy but also shields a substantial portion of items that would otherwise fail under noise. The effect is strongest for synthetic punctuation corruption, moderate for WikiTypo, and still clearly visible for R2ATA.

As shown in Figure 3, accuracy decreases as punctuation intensity rises from Punct-1010 to Punct-5050. This degradation is visible at the single-agent level (n=1n{=}1), where models lose between 5​–​155\text{--}15 percentage points compared to the Clean baseline. However, collaboration rapidly compensates for these losses by n=5n{=}5, the performance gap between Punct-1010 and Clean inputs becomes negligible for most model families, and even Punct-3030 and Punct-5050 recover a substantial share of their accuracy.

Despite the accuracy gains from collaboration, noise affects models similarly. As we can see in Figure 4, the ASR values stay almost the same when increasing the number of agents. This indicates that under simple surface-level perturbations, the collaboration between agents is as vulnerable to noise as a single LLM.

5.2.  Datasets

Figure 5 and Figure 6 reveal distinct robustness profiles by dataset. MATH is the most difficult benchmark in absolute terms. Accuracy starts lowest and improves with more agents, yet gaps to the Clean baseline remain under all types of adversarial inputs even at large agent counts. Its ASR is also the highest among the datasets and hardly declines with increasing nn, indicating that long, multi-step solutions are sensitive to both synthetic punctuation and human-like typos.
For the GSM8K dataset, moving from one to five agents recovers much of the loss from punctuation noise, and ASR drops steadily with nn. WikiTypo consistently induces the largest degradation at a fixed agent count, suggesting heterogeneous human errors are more disruptive than punctuation insertions on these short, compositional problems.
MMLU (math subset) is comparatively stable. Accuracies cluster tightly and rise smoothly with agent count, but its ASR is slightly higher than in GSM8K across noise types.
MULTIARITH is near the ceiling. Accuracy saturates by approximately five agents across all noise types, and ASR is minimal and continues to decrease with nn. The short, structured arithmetic chains offer limited headroom for noise to reduce performance or for collaboration to yield large additional gains.
Overall, easier datasets with simpler tasks (GSM8K, MULTIARITH) are less affected by noise, which is reflected in their lower ASR values. Any performance degradation can be compensated for more easily through multi-agent collaboration. In contrast, more challenging datasets (MATH and MMLU) suffer greater absolute performance drops under noise, and even with larger agent counts, the recovery remains incomplete, highlighting that task difficulty amplifies the impact of input perturbations.

5.3.  Adversarial noise types

Figure 7 presents the Attack Success Rate (ASR) aggregated across datasets, broken down by model family and agent count. Two major patterns emerge. Across all conditions, we observe an almost stable ordering of impact: WikiTypo >> Punct-5050 ≥\geq Punct-3030 ≥\geq R2ATA ≥\geq Punct-1010, with R2ATA typically close to the Clean baseline. This ranking can be more visibly seen in Figure 1.

However, the punctuation noise types as well as R2ATA seem to generally have a similar negative impact on the performance of all the investigated models. This impact is also somewhat stable as we increase the number of agents. By contrast, WikiTypo remains the dominant bottleneck. Even at n=25n{=}25, ASR typically stays above 0.100.10, far higher than for punctuation. Human typos introduce heterogeneous and context-dependent distortions that majority voting cannot fully absorb, making them the most persistent source of errors.

6.  Conclusion

This work provides a systematic study of multi-LLM-agent robustness for question answering under synthetic and human-like input noise. Using a unified sampling-and-voting framework across four datasets (GSM8K, MATH, MMLU–Math, MultiArith) and six open-source models, we examined accuracy and ASR as a function of the number of collaborating agents. Three findings emerge. First, collaboration reliably improves accuracy, with the largest gains between one and five agents and diminishing returns beyond ten. However, ASR remains almost stable as the agent count increases. This pattern holds across models and datasets, indicating that multi-agent collaboration via majority voting is effective in improving accuracy, but the adversarial robustness gap persists.

Second, the noise type matters. Punctuation corruption degrades performance roughly in proportion to its intensity, yet is largely neutralized by five to ten agents. Human typos remain the dominant bottleneck: WikiTypo consistently induces the largest gaps to Clean accuracy and the highest ASR, even at high agent counts. R2ATA occupy a middle ground. Finally, model-level comparisons show that robustness does not strictly correlate with parameter count. While the midsize models show the highest attack success rates, both the larger and the smaller ones show more robustness. Within families such as Qwen and Gemma, larger models consistently achieve lower ASR values and thus demonstrate stronger inherent robustness. Their smaller counterparts show similar robustness while benefiting more from collaboration. Promising directions include noise-aware sampling and aggregation objectives, verifier- or tool-assisted agents, and training-time augmentation targeted at human typos. Extending beyond our scope, open-source models, and character-level corruptions to other domains, languages, and real-world pipelines will test the breadth of these gains.

7.  Limitations

This study has several limitations. First, we restrict evaluation to English, math-reasoning benchmarks, and character-level corruptions; we do not test multilingual data, formatting/layout perturbations (e.g., LaTeX/OCR noise), or adaptive adversaries that react to model outputs. Second, our multi-agent scheme is a single instantiation-independent sampling from the same base model with fixed prompts/decoding and simple majority voting, so we do not compare against debate, tool-augmented agents, verifier-guided aggregation, diversity-promoting sampling, or cost/latency-aware strategies; the efficiency–robustness frontier therefore remains underexplored. Third, answer extraction is based on rule-based numeric parsing. Residual parsing errors can inflate ASR or deflate accuracy. Fourth, all agents share the same base model, so errors can be correlated, and our analysis does not disentangle correlation structure from the benefits of voting.

8.  Ethical Considerations

We evaluate only open-weight LLMs on public math benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, MMLU–Math, MultiArith), which contain no personal or sensitive data. No human subjects were involved. Our findings highlight both the benefits and limitations of multi-agent setups; they should not be interpreted as guarantees of reliability in high-stakes domains. Practitioners must assess risks carefully when transferring these methods beyond research.

10.  Appendix

The following are some of the failure cases under different attacks:

Takeaway: This example shows how punctuation noise can disrupt the model’s reasoning in complex mathematical problems. The model incorrectly assumes that exactly one real root must be a repeated root, leading to a flawed approach and incorrect conclusion. This highlights that noise can cause the model to make invalid assumptions and fail to apply correct mathematical principles.

Takeaway: This example shows how the model can misinterpret the relationship between "destroyed" and "defeated" enemies. Despite correctly calculating that 8 enemies were destroyed, the model incorrectly assumes the 3 remaining enemies are the ones that were "defeated," reversing the logical relationship and leading to an incorrect answer.

Takeaway: This example demonstrates how inserting punctuation noise can lead to task misunderstanding. The original problem intended that James runs 3 sprints, 3 times per week, but the model interpreted it as only 3 sprints total per week, resulting in an incorrect calculation.

Takeaway: This example demonstrates how character substitution noise (R2ATA) can lead to logical inconsistencies in the model’s reasoning. The model correctly identifies Statement 1 as false, but then contradicts itself by stating Statement 2 is true while selecting option (B) which requires both statements to be false, showing confusion in maintaining logical consistency throughout the response.
